editorialTake:
AI is deepening the divide between retail giants and everyone else, not closing it. Amazon’s $200 billion AI bet, defended by CEO Andy Jassy, is not just about future-proofing but about locking in dominance as smaller sellers face new fees and cash crunches that force supplier renegotiations and order delays. Meanwhile, Frasers Group’s AI assistant drove a 25% conversion jump, but Mercor’s $10 billion valuation evaporated overnight after a data breach, reminding us that tech scale-ups can expose operators to new risks as quickly as they promise efficiency.

The promise of AI-powered platforms is seductive, but the reality is uneven. Walmart’s marketplace is surging in general merchandise with AI-driven logistics, while DTC brands going viral on TikTok are buckling under fulfillment failures and spiraling shipping costs. The strongest objection is that AI tools are widely available, so anyone can compete, but the evidence shows the real advantage goes to those with the capital and infrastructure to absorb shocks and invest ahead of the curve.

For luxury and jewellery operators, the lesson is to prioritize resilience over novelty. Invest in supply chain visibility and risk management, not just digital engagement. As AI arms races heat up, the winners will be those who can withstand volatility, not simply those who automate first.
oneSentenceSummary: While AI is touted as a panacea for operational woes, sellers and suppliers are squeezed harder than ever, revealing automation's winners aren't always its users.
